final_answer.key_evidence_summary: Whole-system Network-Drop sweep with NO latency row: all 21 alerted services show TRAFFIC_ANOMALY[Network Drop]+THROUGHPUT_DROP[RPS]; the system's total-traffic chokepoint ts-gateway-service carries the largest traffic (In 667.58->283.68pps, -57.5%; Out 555.19->208.25pps, -62.5%) and the steepest throughput collapse (RPS 5.92->1.30, -78.0%), with its upstream entry ts-ui-dashboard at In 546.08->191.81pps (-64.9%) / RPS -68.0%. Mechanism verbatim, bound to a concrete object: ts-ui-dashboard-554844f867-2z25h is the ONLY pod with RESTARTS=3 (Last State Terminated/Reason: Error/Exit Code 1, event 'Warning BackOff Back-off restarting failed container ts-ui-dashboard'), and its previous container log reads 'nginx: [emerg] host not found in upstream "ts-gateway-service" in /usr/local/openresty/nginx/conf/nginx.conf:41' - i.e. the service name ts-gateway-service could not be resolved by its caller, so the entry hop failed fast (explaining traffic collapse without any latency rise) and recovered (same pod access log later all HTTP 200, POST /api/v1/orderservice/order/refresh 200). Object-layer exclusion: all 42 deployments 1/1 AVAILABLE, all pods 2/2 Running, endpoints bound (ts-gateway-service 172.20.3.215:18888), TCP probes to ts-gateway-service:18888 and ts-ui-dashboard:8080 succeed from worker-01/02/03, all nodes Ready with no taints/pressure and affected services spread across all three workers (no node-scope fault); the gateway route table in configmap ts-gateway-service-config has every Path<->uri pairing correct (no misroute). The broken artifact is the DNS name of ts-gateway-service, the system's total-traffic convergence point, whose collapse radiates as the namespace-wide drop.

This wording lives on the metric surface — the alerts name the case, and the object layer is only the exclusion. Read the alerts first, and the case you land on decides:

1. **Alerts first.** `GetAlerts` tells you whose anomaly it is, which kind (latency / saturation / throughput / traffic), and at what scope. Unlike the reachability wordings, opening from the object layer here is not troubleshooting — the signal is in the metrics. When several alerts fire at once the case is the **primary anomaly** — the service the other alerts ripple from, carrying the runaway deviation: read the rows' shape before their size — a latency row that moves only its p90 is a partial-traffic ripple (only the traffic sharing a path with the degraded pod slowed), while the row whose p50 and p90 both move carries the delay across all of its traffic and marks the epicenter; among those both-percentile rows the epicenter carries the steepest p90 escalation (measured baselines only), and the graph closes it (`GetServiceDependencies`). Then settle the pick in this order — branches (a) then (b):
   - **(a) Two moving rows on one call path:** if one moving row's service sits downstream of another moving row's service on the walk, **the downstream one is the source — whatever the row shapes say**: the upstream row is its accumulated wait on the callee, and a leaf that moves only its p90 is a delay riding the leaf's own path (the p90-only-is-ripple reading is for rows with no moving row downstream of them). This also settles a zeroed-baseline pair (`New Spike`, nothing else to rank by) — the downstream one is the source.
   - **(b) Independent candidates (no call path between them):** every ripple is its direct neighbor, so a candidate that would need a quiet intermediate hop is not the source; the dual-moving row is the epicenter and a p90-only row is a partial-traffic ripple — among the dual rows the steepest p90 escalation takes it. Percentages on near-zero baselines prove nothing. A saturation row counts only when it rides on that epicenter **and comes with the service's own latency rise** — a genuine resource fault shows the throttle *and* its own latency climbing together; a bare `cpu_cfs` row on a service that is not the epicenter, with no latency of its own, is collateral noise — don't out-rank the runaway deviation with it. **And when no latency row is in the set at all — the alerts read as bare saturation — the case is not on the saturation surface: a `Val: … (Throttled)` with no normal to compare against shows no movement (a chronically throttled value reads the same before and after), and sub-core percentages are sub-noise; the row that carries an actual deviation beyond saturation — a traffic / network move — is the one that names the service.** A `LATENCY_MISSING` row ("metrics dropped to zero/NaN") is a hole the collection left in the injection window, not a service's deviation — it never names the case, so don't anchor on it. And when a whole-system network-drop sweep carries no latency row at all, the epicenter is the point every request flows through (the system's total traffic) — its collapse is the source, the rest is the ripple. Apply the branches below to the primary anomaly, not to the loudest keyword.
2. **Deal with the case you land on:**
   - **Saturation rows on one service** (`RESOURCE_SATURATION [cpu_cfs]` / `[cpu core]` / memory) → it's a resource fault on that service's pods: read its pods face (usage vs limits) to close.
   - **A constant delay riding on one service's own latency** — its p50/p90 jump by a fixed amount, its callers see the same added delay, its downstream server-side latencies stay clean, no saturation rows → `pod_network_delay`: the delay sits on that pod's network path. Don't reach for a code explanation — an artificial delay *in code* is a code-defect (a different wording, and it has to be shown from the code surface); under this wording a delay case is network-side.
   - **The same latency / packet anomaly across every pod on one node** (scope it with the pods listing's NODE column) → it's a node-scope network fault: read the node objects (conditions / node runtime services) to close.
3. **Close by excluding the object layer.** The pods / deployments / services / endpoints / nodes listings show everything else healthy — RESTARTS 0, AVAILABLE 1/1, endpoints bound, nodes Ready, no mechanism events. apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  namespace: train-ticket
  name: ts-gateway-service
spec:
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: ts-gateway-service
  replicas: 1
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: ts-gateway-service
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: ts-gateway-service
        image: ghcr.io/sregym/ts-gateway-service:latest
        imagePullPolicy: IfNotPresent
        env:
        - name: SPRING_MAIN_ALLOW_CIRCULAR_REFERENCES
          value: 'true'
        - name: NODE_IP
          valueFrom:
            fieldRef:
              fieldPath: status.hostIP
        envFrom:
        - configMapRef:
            name: nacos
        ports:
        - containerPort: 18888
        resources:
          requests:
            cpu: 200m
            memory: 350Mi
          limits:
            cpu: 500m
            memory: 512Mi
        readinessProbe:
          tcpSocket:
            port: 18888
          initialDelaySeconds: 60
          periodSeconds: 10
          timeoutSeconds: 5
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  namespace: train-ticket
  name: ts-gateway-service
spec:
  ports:
  - name: http
    port: 18888
    nodePort: 30467
  selector:
    app: ts-gateway-service
  type: NodePort
